# Exercise 9.3 — One toolbox for explanations: DALEX {#sec-dalex}

Exercises 9.1 and 9.2 used a different package for each explanation. The
**DALEX** package puts them behind one interface. You wrap the fitted model
once in an **explainer**, then ask the explainer each question. The package
exists in R (with **DALEXtra** for tidymodels) and in Python (`dalex`), with
the same function names.

::: {.callout-note}
## The plots are for looking at
The code for every plot is folded away just above it, in case you are curious,
and all of it is in the notebook linked at the top of each tab. You are not
expected to write it yourself.
:::

:::::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

### Packages and data

```{r}
# Packages for this exercise. If one is missing, remove the # and run this line once:
# install.packages(c("tidyverse", "tidymodels", "DALEX", "DALEXtra", "ranger"))

library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(DALEX)                 # explanations for any model
library(DALEXtra)              # connects DALEX to tidymodels

theme_set(theme_bw())          # white background for every plot
options(pillar.sigfig = 3)     # show three significant figures in tables
```

The data are the 750 people in
[`data/diabetes_clean.csv`](data/diabetes_clean.csv), as in Exercises 9.1 and
9.2. The outcome is `diabetes` (`neg` or `pos`); the predictors are pregnant,
glucose, mass, pedigree and age, in their own units. As always, 80% of the
people are used for training and 20% are held back as the test set.

```{r}
diabetes <- read_csv("data/diabetes_clean.csv") |>
  select(pregnant, glucose, mass, pedigree, age, diabetes) |>
  mutate(diabetes = factor(diabetes, levels = c("neg", "pos")))

set.seed(42)
split <- initial_split(diabetes, prop = 0.8)
train <- training(split)
test  <- testing(split)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 1 — The model and the explainer

The black box is the random forest of Exercises 9.1 and 9.2. Fit it on the
training rows:

```{r}
rf_spec <- rand_forest(trees = 500) |>
  set_engine("ranger", importance = "impurity") |>
  set_mode("classification")

set.seed(1)
rf_fit <- rf_spec |>
  fit(diabetes ~ ., data = train)
```

Evaluate it once on the test set:

```{r}
test_preds <- test |>
  bind_cols(predict(rf_fit, new_data = test, type = "prob"),
            predict(rf_fit, new_data = test))

test_preds |> accuracy(truth = diabetes, estimate = .pred_class)
test_preds |> roc_auc(truth = diabetes, .pred_pos, event_level = "second")
```

Accuracy 0.720 and AUC 0.753 on the 150 test patients.

Now wrap the model in an explainer. `explain_tidymodels()` needs the model,
the predictors of the people to explain it on (the test patients), and the
true outcome `y` **as numbers, 1 for diabetes and 0 for none**.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
explainer <- explain_tidymodels(
  rf_fit,
  data  = test |> select(-diabetes),
  y     = as.numeric(test$diabetes == ______),   # 1 = diabetes, 0 = none
  label = "Random forest",
  verbose = FALSE                                # no progress report
)
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
`y` must be 1 for the people with diabetes. Which level of `diabetes` is that?
`as.numeric(test$diabetes)` on its own would give 1 and **2** (the positions
of the levels), and every explanation would then be wrong.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
explainer <- explain_tidymodels(
  rf_fit,
  data  = test |> select(-diabetes),
  y     = as.numeric(test$diabetes == "pos"),
  label = "Random forest",
  verbose = FALSE                                # no progress report
)
```
:::
:::

A quick check that the explainer is set up right: its AUC should be the one
you just computed.

```{r}
model_performance(explainer)$measures |> as.data.frame()
```

It is, 0.753.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 2 — Which variables matter?

`model_parts()` is the **permutation importance** of Exercise 9.1: shuffle one
variable in the test set, see how much worse the model gets, repeat 10 times
and average. DALEX measures "worse" as $1 - \text{AUC}$, so a larger number is
a worse model. `_full_model_` is the value with nothing shuffled.

```{r}
set.seed(1)
importance_dalex <- model_parts(explainer)

importance_dalex |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  filter(permutation == 0) |>        # permutation 0 is the average of the 10 shuffles
  select(variable, dropout_loss)
```

With nothing shuffled the loss is 0.247. Shuffling glucose raises it to
0.380; shuffling any other variable raises it by 0.033 at most (BMI). Glucose
is by far the most important variable, as in Exercise 9.1, and here it took
one line of code.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 3 — How does the prediction change with glucose?

An importance says *how much* a variable matters, not *how*. For one patient,
set her glucose to 57, then a little higher, and so on up to 194, keep everything else about
her as it is, and predict each time. The curve you get is her **ICE profile**
(individual conditional expectation). The average of the 150 ICE profiles is
the **partial dependence profile**: what the model predicts, on average, at
each glucose level. `model_profile()` computes both.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
pdp_glucose <- model_profile(explainer, variables = ______, type = "partial",
                             N = NULL,                         # use all 150 patients
                             variable_splits_type = "uniform") # an evenly spaced grid
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
Give the name of the variable as a string, in quotes.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
pdp_glucose <- model_profile(explainer, variables = "glucose", type = "partial",
                             N = NULL,                         # use all 150 patients
                             variable_splits_type = "uniform") # an evenly spaced grid
```
:::
:::

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for this plot (optional)"
#| fig-height: 3.5
pdp_glucose$cp_profiles |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  ggplot(aes(x = glucose, y = `_yhat_`, group = `_ids_`)) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey60", alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_line(data = pdp_glucose$agr_profiles,
            aes(x = `_x_`, y = `_yhat_`, group = NULL),
            colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(x = "Glucose (mg/dL)", y = "Predicted probability of diabetes",
       title = "ICE profiles (grey) and partial dependence (blue)")
```

**Question!** Describe the blue curve in words. Do all the grey curves have
the same shape?

Below a glucose of about 100 the average prediction stays low, between 0.14
and 0.24. It climbs gradually to about 0.40 at 140, rises steeply between 145
and 157 to about 0.68, and stays between 0.66 and 0.73 above that. The steps
come from the forest's splits. Every grey curve ends higher than it starts, but they start at different
heights (from 0.07 to 0.47) and rise by very different amounts (from 0.15 to
0.75). How much
glucose matters depends on a patient's other values; the average curve hides
that.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 4 — One patient

`predict_parts()` explains one prediction. Take the first test patient:

```{r}
new_observation <- test |>
  slice(1) |>
  select(-diabetes)

new_observation
predict(explainer, new_observation)          # her predicted probability
```

Ask for her **SHAP values**, as in Exercise 9.2. DALEX estimates them from 25
random orders of the variables, with the test patients as the background.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
set.seed(1)
shap_patient <- predict_parts(explainer, new_observation = new_observation,
                              type = ______, B = 25)

shap_patient |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  filter(B == 0) |>                    # B = 0 holds the average of the 25 orders
  select(variable, contribution) |>
  arrange(desc(abs(contribution)))
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
The type is a string, the name of the method in lower case. See
`?predict_parts`.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
set.seed(1)
shap_patient <- predict_parts(explainer, new_observation = new_observation,
                              type = "shap", B = 25)

shap_patient |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  filter(B == 0) |>                    # B = 0 holds the average of the 25 orders
  select(variable, contribution) |>
  arrange(desc(abs(contribution)))
```
:::
:::

She is 28, with a glucose of 194, and the forest gives her 0.706. The
average prediction over the test patients is 0.379. Her glucose adds +0.361;
each of the other four variables moves it by 0.04 or less. As
in Exercise 9.2, the contributions add up from the average to her prediction.
With `type = "break_down"` DALEX adds the variables in one fixed order instead
of averaging over many.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Key points
- Wrap the fitted model once in an explainer, with the test patients and `y` coded 1 for diabetes and 0 for none. Every explanation is then one function call.
- `model_parts()` is the permutation importance of Exercise 9.1: glucose matters most.
- `model_profile()` gives the partial dependence profile (the average) and the ICE profiles (one per patient) for one variable. Read both: the average can hide patients who differ.
- `predict_parts()` explains one patient, with SHAP values as in Exercise 9.2.
:::

### Packages and data

```{python}
# Packages for this exercise. If one is missing, install it once from a terminal
# (in a Jupyter notebook, type %pip instead of pip):
# pip install pandas numpy matplotlib scikit-learn "dalex>=1.8"

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import dalex as dx             # explanations for any model

from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, roc_auc_score
```

The data are the 750 people in
[`data/diabetes_clean.csv`](data/diabetes_clean.csv), as in Exercises 9.1 and
9.2. The outcome is `diabetes`, coded 1 for `pos` and 0 for `neg`; the
predictors are pregnant, glucose, mass, pedigree and age, in their own units.
As always, 80% of the people are used for training and 20% are held back as
the test set.

```{python}
diabetes = pd.read_csv("data/diabetes_clean.csv")
diabetes = diabetes[["pregnant", "glucose", "mass", "pedigree", "age", "diabetes"]]
diabetes["diabetes"] = (diabetes["diabetes"] == "pos").astype(int)       # 1 = pos, 0 = neg

predictors = ["pregnant", "glucose", "mass", "pedigree", "age"]

train, test = train_test_split(diabetes, test_size=0.2, random_state=42)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 1 — The model and the explainer

The black box is the random forest of Exercises 9.1 and 9.2. Fit it on the
training rows:

```{python}
rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=500, random_state=1)
rf = rf.fit(train[predictors], train["diabetes"])
```

Evaluate it once on the test set:

```{python}
test_class = rf.predict(test[predictors])                # predicted class, threshold 0.5
test_prob  = rf.predict_proba(test[predictors])[:, 1]    # probability of diabetes

print("accuracy:", round(accuracy_score(test["diabetes"], test_class), 3))
print("AUC:     ", round(roc_auc_score(test["diabetes"], test_prob), 3))
```

Accuracy 0.713 and AUC 0.794 on the 150 test patients.

Now wrap the model in an explainer. `dx.Explainer()` needs the model, the
predictors of the people to explain it on (the test patients), and the true
outcome `y` **as numbers, 1 for diabetes and 0 for none**.

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
explainer = dx.Explainer(
    rf,
    data=test[______],
    y=test["diabetes"],                           # already 1 = diabetes, 0 = none
    label="Random forest",
    verbose=False,                                # no progress report
)
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
`data` is the table of predictors only, without the outcome column: the same
columns the forest was fitted on.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
explainer = dx.Explainer(
    rf,
    data=test[predictors],
    y=test["diabetes"],                           # already 1 = diabetes, 0 = none
    label="Random forest",
    verbose=False,                                # no progress report
)
```
:::
:::

A quick check that the explainer is set up right: its AUC should be the one
you just computed.

```{python}
explainer.model_performance().result.round(3)
```

It is, 0.794.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 2 — Which variables matter?

`model_parts()` is the **permutation importance** of Exercise 9.1: shuffle one
variable in the test set, see how much worse the model gets, repeat 10 times
and average. DALEX measures "worse" as $1 - \text{AUC}$, so a larger number is
a worse model. `_full_model_` is the value with nothing shuffled.

```{python}
importance_dalex = explainer.model_parts(random_state=1)

importance_dalex.result[["variable", "dropout_loss"]].round(3)
```

With nothing shuffled the loss is 0.206. Shuffling glucose raises it to
0.352; shuffling any other variable raises it by 0.036 at most (age), and
shuffling pedigree changes it by less than 0.001. Glucose is by far the most
important variable, as in Exercise 9.1, and here it took one line of code.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 3 — How does the prediction change with glucose?

An importance says *how much* a variable matters, not *how*. For one patient,
set her glucose to 73, then a little higher, and so on up to 196, keep everything else about
her as it is, and predict each time. The curve you get is her **ICE profile**
(individual conditional expectation). The average of the 150 ICE profiles is
the **partial dependence profile**: what the model predicts, on average, at
each glucose level. `model_profile()` computes both.

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
pdp_glucose = explainer.model_profile(variables=[______], type="partial",
                                      verbose=False)
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
Give the name of the variable as a string, in quotes, inside the list.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
pdp_glucose = explainer.model_profile(variables=["glucose"], type="partial",
                                      verbose=False)
```
:::
:::

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for this plot (optional)"
#| fig-height: 3.5
ice = pdp_glucose.raw_profiles.result

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5))
for patient_id in ice["_ids_"].unique():
    one = ice[ice["_ids_"] == patient_id]
    ax.plot(one["glucose"], one["_yhat_"], color="grey", alpha=0.3, linewidth=0.7)
ax.plot(pdp_glucose.result["_x_"], pdp_glucose.result["_yhat_"], color="steelblue", linewidth=2.5)
ax.set_xlabel("Glucose (mg/dL)")
ax.set_ylabel("Predicted probability of diabetes")
ax.set_title("ICE profiles (grey) and partial dependence (blue)")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

**Question!** Describe the blue curve in words. Do all the grey curves have
the same shape?

Below a glucose of about 100 the average prediction stays low, between 0.15
and 0.20. It climbs gradually to about 0.37 at 140, rises steeply between 145
and 157 to about 0.66, and stays between 0.63 and 0.67 above that. The steps
come from the forest's splits. Every grey curve ends higher than it
starts, but they start at different heights (from 0.04 to 0.64) and rise by
very different amounts (from 0.08 to 0.85). How much glucose matters depends on a patient's other values;
the average curve hides that.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 4 — One patient

`predict_parts()` explains one prediction. Take the first test patient:

```{python}
new_observation = test[predictors].iloc[[0]]

print(new_observation)
print(explainer.predict(new_observation))     # her predicted probability
```

Ask for her **SHAP values**, as in Exercise 9.2. DALEX estimates them from 25
random orders of the variables, with the test patients as the background.

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
shap_patient = explainer.predict_parts(new_observation, type=______, B=25,
                                       random_state=1)

shap_average = shap_patient.result[shap_patient.result["B"] == 0]   # B = 0 holds the average of the 25 orders
shap_average = shap_average[["variable", "contribution"]]
shap_average.sort_values("contribution", key=abs, ascending=False).round(3)
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
The type is a string, the name of the method in lower case. See
`help(explainer.predict_parts)`.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
shap_patient = explainer.predict_parts(new_observation, type="shap", B=25,
                                       random_state=1)

shap_average = shap_patient.result[shap_patient.result["B"] == 0]   # B = 0 holds the average of the 25 orders
shap_average = shap_average[["variable", "contribution"]]
shap_average.sort_values("contribution", key=abs, ascending=False).round(3)
```
:::
:::

This split puts a different person first than the R split does. She is 35,
with a glucose of 115, and the forest gives her 0.276. The average prediction
over the test patients is 0.356. Her glucose pulls the prediction down by
0.144; each of the other four variables moves it by 0.036 or less. As in
Exercise 9.2, the contributions add up from the average to her prediction.
With `type="break_down"` DALEX adds the variables in one fixed order instead
of averaging over many.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Key points
- Wrap the fitted model once in an explainer, with the test patients and `y` coded 1 for diabetes and 0 for none. Every explanation is then one function call.
- `model_parts()` is the permutation importance of Exercise 9.1: glucose matters most.
- `model_profile()` gives the partial dependence profile (the average) and the ICE profiles (one per patient) for one variable. Read both: the average can hide patients who differ.
- `predict_parts()` explains one patient, with SHAP values as in Exercise 9.2.
:::

::::::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::: {.instructor}
**Teaching choice.** Four key messages only: build the explainer once, then
ask it for permutation importance (Exercise 9.1's idea), the glucose partial
dependence with its ICE profiles, and one patient's SHAP values (Exercise
9.2's idea). The model is unchanged from the other Day 9 chapters (five
predictors, `rand_forest(trees = 500)` with ranger, `set.seed(1)`;
`RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=500, random_state=1)`); only the split
is now the module's random 80/20 split. The plots are drawn with ggplot2 /
matplotlib from the result tables, because DALEX's own `plot()` methods print
deprecation warnings in R and draw plotly figures in Python. `y` is
`as.numeric(test$diabetes == "pos")`: the original page's `as.numeric()` of a
factor gives 1 and 2. Break-down, the pedigree and age profiles and the
modelStudio / Arena dashboards were cut; mention them if time allows.

**Expected values.** Split 600/150; R and Python draw different splits and
quote their own numbers. R: test accuracy 0.720, AUC 0.753 (the explainer's
AUC is the same). `model_parts()` loss (1 − AUC, 10 shuffles, `set.seed(1)`):
full 0.247, pregnant 0.248, age 0.255, pedigree 0.259, mass 0.280, glucose
0.380, baseline 0.477. Glucose partial dependence (grid 57 to 194): 0.14 to
0.24 below 100, about 0.40 at 140, about 0.68 at 157, 0.66 to 0.73 above.
ICE profiles start at 0.07 to 0.47 and end 0.15 to 0.75 higher. First test
patient: age 28, glucose 194, pedigree 0.24, BMI 28.5, no pregnancies, `neg`;
predicted 0.706, mean prediction 0.379; SHAP (B = 25) glucose +0.361,
pedigree −0.040, age +0.034, mass −0.018, pregnant −0.009. Python: test
accuracy 0.713, AUC 0.794. `model_parts()` loss: pedigree 0.205, full 0.206,
pregnant 0.218, mass 0.234, age 0.242, glucose 0.352, baseline 0.517. Glucose
partial dependence (grid 73 to 196): 0.15 to 0.20 below 100, about 0.37 at
140, about 0.66 at 157, 0.63 to 0.67 above. ICE profiles start at 0.04 to
0.64 and end 0.08 to 0.85 higher. First test patient: age 35, glucose 115,
pedigree 0.368, BMI 28.8, 6 pregnancies, `neg`; predicted 0.276, mean
prediction 0.356; SHAP glucose −0.144, age +0.036, mass +0.021, pregnant
+0.018, pedigree −0.012.

**Common failures.** (1) `y = as.numeric(test$diabetes)`, giving 1/2; the
residuals then have a mean of about 1 instead of about 0. (2)
Passing the full test table, outcome included, as `data`. (3) In R, leaving
`N` at its default of 100 in `model_profile()`: it then samples 100 of the
150 patients and the curve changes from run to run. (4) Expecting the same
first patient in R and Python. (5) Reading a small negative change in loss
(Python, pedigree) as the variable hurting the model: it is noise.

**Timing.** Part 1 fifteen minutes, Part 2 ten, Part 3 fifteen, Part 4 ten.
:::
:::
